subject: Cooking
title: Sourdough's COVID-19 Comeback
description: A micro-lesson that makes Sourdough's COVID-19 Comeback usable.

hook.text: In March 2020, flour vanished from supermarket shelves. Social media flooded with sourdough selfies.

buildup.text: Locked-down workers with time and anxiety turned to bread-baking — sourdough became a pandemic coping mechanism.

discovery.text: Google searches for 'sourdough starter' increased 500%. YouTube bread tutorials gained millions of views overnight.

twist.text: Most pandemic bakers quit within months. But a lasting 15% increase in home baking persisted post-lockdown.

climax.text: The pandemic reconnected millions with a 5,000-year-old skill — and many discovered they loved it.

punchline.text: A virus brought back the world's oldest comfort food.

quiz.question: By how much did 'sourdough starter' Google searches increase during COVID-19?

details.summary: During 2020 COVID lockdowns, sourdough baking exploded worldwide as homebound people turned to bread as therapy, creative outlet, and self-sufficiency. Flour sold out globally. Social media filled with sourdough starter photos.
details.whyItMatters: The sourdough boom revealed bread-making's deep psychological role. In crisis, humans return to the most fundamental food craft, finding comfort, control, and community through shared baking.
takeaways: Flour shortages occurred worldwide during spring 2020 lockdowns
Social media sourdough culture created a global baking community
Baking served as stress relief and a sense of productive control

faq.question: Why did so many people choose sourdough during lockdowns?
faq.answer: Sourdough requires only flour, water, and salt — no commercial yeast, which sold out immediately. The multi-day process gave homebound people a structured activity. Feeding a starter felt like nurturing something alive. Social media sharing created community during isolation.

faq.question: Did the sourdough trend last after lockdowns ended?
faq.answer: Interest declined from peak levels but remained significantly above pre-pandemic baselines. Many people maintained starters and continued baking. Flour companies reported permanently higher home baking sales. The trend introduced a generation to fermentation and artisan techniques.
